tweets.text:
OpenAI published a preprint with wet-lab results for proteins designed by its GPT-6 models, using only reasoning and code. No specialized biology model generated the designs.

The results change a lot depending on the experiment. Minibinders built from GPT-6.2's 3D designs: 322 tested against 5 targets, 35 bound (10.9%), with at least one hit on every target. When it redesigned the loops of six small antibodies, 128 of 182 designs (70%) showed binding to IL-4Rα. On therapeutic antibody fragments, where it had to change about half the amino acids in three loops, 179 of 272 (66%) kept binding.

OpenAI lists the limits itself. Specialized models still supplied the sequences and picked which candidates went to the lab. The original RFdiffusion study reported higher hit rates. Predicting a full protein structure is still a clear weakness.

So this isn't a drug, and they don't claim it is. A general model did the design step that usually needs a dedicated tool, and the lab found real binders. I'd like to see the same test with the internal model that scored higher on their computational benchmarks.
